paragraphs.source_en: In 2000, this magnet school was really struggling, and Muriel Summers had just been appointed principal. Attendance was exceptionally low: the school could accommodate 800 students, but only 300 students were enrolled. The building was messy. Parents were not involved. The teachers didn’t enjoy working there, and the kids could sense this. Finally, the superintendent said, “Muriel, we’re going to shut you down as a magnet school because you’re not attracting enough students.” Muriel was desperate and didn’t know what to do. She asked the superintendent, “Can I have another year?” He said, “I’ll give you another week to come up with a new idea.”

paragraphs.source_en: Muriel challenged the school staff: *Why don’t we go out and talk* *with the community to find out what they want the school to teach their kids?* She and her team talked with parents and employers. They said, “We want our children to be self-starters. We want them to get along well with other people—to learn how to set goals, solve problems, balance their lives, show up on time, resolve conflicts, and play at the park.” They talked about what we might call leadership skills, or twenty-first-century life skills. Nobody said anything about higher test scores.

paragraphs.source_en: After synthesizing all of these experiences, Muriel Summers and her staff came to feel that “leadership” was what their school needed most. Their superintendent liked it. And their new mission statement was posted in the center of the school: *Our mission is to develop leaders one child at a time.* The mission was not meant to make students into future CEOs; it was to help them become leaders of their own lives and in their school.
